A good engineer doesn't just fix the problem. A great engineer understands WHY it happened. 💡

In Engineering and Programming, debugging is much more than finding an error and changing a line of code.
It's about developing a systematic way of thinking.

Whether you're working with Embedded Systems, Software Development, or Artificial Intelligence, an effective debugging mindset can make all the difference.

🔍 Here are 4 habits every engineer should develop:

1️⃣ Reproduce the problem
Understand when and why the issue occurs before attempting to fix it.

2️⃣ Isolate the root cause
Break the problem into smaller parts. Don't assume the first visible symptom is the actual cause.

3️⃣ Test one hypothesis at a time
Make controlled changes and observe their impact instead of changing multiple things simultaneously.

4️⃣ Verify the solution
Make sure the fix addresses the root cause without introducing new issues.

🚀 Technical knowledge helps you write code, but analytical thinking helps you solve real-world engineering challenges.

posts.text:
Huge numbers of players have already preloaded GTA 6. None of them can play it until it unlocks on November 19.

Here's the engineering behind that, and why it's smart.

1. Spread the load
GTA 6 needs over 200 GB on PS5. If millions of players started downloading at launch, the servers would struggle. So Rockstar opened preloads about a week early, and the heavy download gets spread across days instead of hours.

2. Lock the files
The downloaded game is encrypted. Without the key, it's just unusable data sitting on your drive.

3. Unlock with something tiny
On launch day, the console only needs a small permission check to decrypt the game, so each player needs only a tiny amount of data on launch day instead of 200+ GB.

"Can't someone just guess the key?"
Not realistically. Consoles use industry-standard encryption like AES. A 128-bit key has about 3.4 × 10³⁸ possible values. Even a machine trying a billion billion (10¹⁸) keys per second would need around 10 trillion years. The universe is about 14 billion years old.

When games do leak early, it's through security bugs, insiders, or early retail copies, not by guessing the key.

The takeaway for engineers:
Don't solve a peak-load problem only by buying bigger servers. Move the heavy work earlier, and keep only the small, critical step for the moment it matters.

Note: This isn't based on official details from Rockstar. It's my understanding as a software engineer of how console preloads typically work.

🧵 GSD: Is It Really the Perfect Solution for Garment Manufacturing?

In the garment industry, we always talk about productivity, efficiency, SMV, and line balancing.

But how accurately do we measure the time required to complete an operation?

This is where GSD (General Sewing Data) comes into play.

GSD is a Predetermined Motion Time System (PMTS) that breaks down sewing operations into basic movements and assigns predetermined time values to them.

Instead of relying entirely on stopwatch observations, it provides a systematic approach to developing standard operation times.

But like every engineering tool, GSD has both advantages and limitations.

Let's take a closer look. 👇

✅ Advantages of GSD

1. More Scientific Time Measurement
It uses predefined motion data rather than depending entirely on individual stopwatch observations.

2. Consistency in SMV
It helps establish consistent time standards when the same method and working conditions are applied.

3. Better Line Balancing
Accurate operation breakdown helps IE professionals distribute workloads more effectively.

4. Improved Production Planning
Reliable standard times support manpower planning, capacity calculation, and target setting.

5. Better Cost Estimation
Accurate operation times help estimate labor costs and support pricing decisions.

6. Method Improvement
Breaking operations into smaller elements helps identify unnecessary movements and opportunities for improvement.

❌ Disadvantages of GSD

1. Requires Specialized Knowledge
Without proper training, understanding and applying GSD correctly can be difficult.

2. Time-Consuming Process
Detailed operation breakdown and coding can require considerable time and effort.

3. Software & Licensing Costs
Professional GSD systems may involve significant investment.

4. Depends on the Correct Working Method
If the operation method, machine setup, or workplace arrangement is incorrect, the calculated standard may not reflect actual production conditions.

5. Not Always Suitable for Every Activity
Some unusual, highly variable, or non-sewing operations may require other work-measurement approaches.

6. Requires Practical Validation
An engineered time should not automatically be treated as achievable without checking actual workplace conditions, operator capability, and method consistency.

🎯 My Take as an IE Professional

GSD is a powerful tool, but having GSD software alone doesn't make someone a good Industrial Engineer.

An effective IE must understand:

- The actual sewing method.
- Machine and attachment requirements.
- Operator skill and capability.
- Workplace layout and material flow.
- Practical production conditions.

Technology provides the standard, but engineering judgment makes it practical.

Finally met my AI crush last week!

I am convinced that Lauren from xAI started the third revolution for coding agents and that it will soon also reach knowledge work agents. Last week, I finally got to meet her in person.

In March 2024, Cursor launched the tab autocomplete model. It was a game changer for software engineers. Tab, tab, tab. Done. That marked revolution 1.0.

Then, in November 2025, Opus 4.5 came out. Another revolution for software engineers. You could describe your problem in plain English, and the model would write the code end to end. At this point, the engineer was still in the loop to check the final result. It became obvious that the engineer was now the bottleneck. GitHub started having more outages.

In August 2026, Lauren started talking about her new Grokbot coding setup. Instead of driving the coding agents herself, she has another agent that instructs and monitors her coding agents. This marks the coding revolution 3.0. Her job now is to define the goal and provide enough guardrails in the codebase so that agents can work safely within it.

Over the span of just two years, the role of an engineer changed drastically: from carefully watching autocomplete suggestions to providing guardrails and high-level goals for agents. Her job didn't get any less demanding. Setting the right guardrails and goals for coding agents requires a strong understanding of the system architecture. Her judgment compounds much faster now.

Coding is an easily verifiable domain, which is why agents find the most success here. I am convinced that business agents will follow soon, with a few important tweaks. I'll write a separate article about the infrastructure requirements that need to be in place for business agents to adopt the same pattern and see the same success.

I'm a little alarmed to read about Product Managers shipping their own code, especially generated code.

LLMs risk reducing each of those roles to its visible veneer. Anyone who doesn't understand why a function exists needs to get that understanding before they make decisions about it.

posts.text:
Most software engineers use MVC as their default architecture.

They believe the framework already chose the best architecture for them.

Then the product grows and the codebase is a mess.

So they adopt an architecture, and get that wrong too.

Here are the 10 most common misconceptions about software architecture.

1. They add layers nobody asked for.

Every layer is a bet that the code behind it will outlive the code in front of it.

The bet pays when the same use case runs from HTTP, a queue and a CLI command, and tests can't reach a business rule without booting the framework.

If none of that is true, skip the layers.

2. They apply one architecture to every module.

A hotel's housekeeping module gets a port, an adapter and a second Room class to change one column from DIRTY to CLEAN.

Answer the architecture question per module.

3. They treat Hexagonal, Clean and Vertical Slice as rivals.

Hexagonal and Clean decide which code can depend on which.

Vertical Slice decides which folder a file lives in.

Combine them and write it down: slices for the folders, Hexagonal rules inside each slice.

4. They trust the folder names instead of the imports.

A class sits in Domain/ and imports an Eloquent model.

Read the use statements, because the folder names can lie.

5. They expect a boundary to make the tests faster on its own.

The suite gets slower when every test still boots the framework and hits a real database.

The boundary tells you which test goes where: rules against fakes, adapters against the real database, and one thin end-to-end test per feature.

6. They read "no framework in the core" as "no Laravel classes".

"Is this Laravel?" is the wrong question.

Ask what you would rewrite if a package disappeared tomorrow.

7. They pay to keep the framework swappable.

Swapping a framework is rare.

The boundary buys core tests that boot no framework and upgrades that stay in the adapters.

8. They reach for microservices to get boundaries.

The boundaries microservices enforce over the network can be enforced inside one codebase.

Start with a modular monolith and extract a service later if scale forces it.

9. They plan a rewrite or a feature freeze.

Big-bang refactors run long and ship in a worse state than they started.

Build new features in the new shape and clean up old code when you touch it.

10. They think anything beyond MVC is complex, with too many files.

In the default layout, cancelling a reservation already touches eight files in eight folders.

A slice keeps one feature in one folder, so a change touches one place.

Architectures, my 15-lesson course, covers every one of these misconceptions.

On 6 and 7 November 2026, we hosted the LLMNetOps Main Workshop in Malang.

40 network engineers and IT professionals from 24 institutions across Indonesia, from Aceh to Ambon, joined us for two days of hands-on activities.

The workshop focused on a practical question: how can campus network teams use locally deployed AI to support their daily work without giving up control of their systems and data?

- On the first day, participants discussed operational challenges, set up a virtual network lab, and installed the LLMNetOps stack alongside an open-weight LLM that could run on their own laptops.

- On the second day, participants used the virtual network lab, which represented a campus network, to work through two simulated network incidents with LLMNetOps. They also explored potential applications in cybersecurity and other campus operations.

LLMNetOps is a self-hosted AI co-pilot for network operations. An engineer can describe an issue in natural language, such as "Users in Building A cannot get an IP address. Check the router." The agent can inspect authorized devices, gather diagnostic information, and present findings for the operator to review. It is designed to run on institutional infrastructure, so sensitive network data can remain under the institution's control.

A principle behind this work is that engineers remain responsible for operational decisions. LLMNetOps is intended to help them investigate problems and handle routine tasks, especially when campus IT teams are working with limited staff and growing demands.

Before the main workshop, we piloted the materials with three institutions in Malang. Their feedback helped us improve the exercises. It was rewarding to see participants, including some with no previous AI experience, deploy and use the platform themselves.

My thanks to Widy Widyawan from Universitas Gadjah Mada for representing IDREN; to my fellow speakers and the development team fromUniversity of Brawijaya IT; theFaculty of Computer Science (FILKOM) University of Brawijaya; to the organizing committee and our three pilot institutions; and to everyone who participated.

This project is supported by a grant from the APNIC Foundation through ISIF Asia 2025 fund.

Participants are now preparing to bring what they learned back to their institutions. We will continue with online follow-up workshops as they begin deployment. We are also progressively releasing LLMNetOps components and supporting materials as open-source software on GitHub.
